edges.description: Perturbed microtubule function in oligodendrocytes compromises the microtubule-dependent transport required to build and maintain myelin.
The same lesion drives degeneration of basal ganglia and cerebellar neurons, an arm that is separate from the myelin arm rather than downstream of it.
Failure of oligodendrocyte myelin production produces the hypomyelination seen on MRI.
Loss of myelinated tract function contributes to the progressive pyramidal, extrapyramidal, cerebellar and bulbar findings.
Basal ganglia degeneration produces the extrapyramidal movement disorder that dominates most presentations.
Cerebellar degeneration produces ataxia, intention tremor and dysmetria.
The structural correlate of the cerebellar arm.
Extrapyramidal and cerebellar degeneration contribute to the progressive decline in motor and bulbar function.
Loss of previously acquired milestones is the presenting event in the late-infantile form.
Motor decline typically costs independent walking.
Models the recurrent human H-ABC allele, and the allelic series isolates the mutant-to-wild-type ratio as the severity determinant.
edges.limitations: Mouse myelination timing and lifespan differ from human, and the treated genotype (D249N over a null) has a mutant-to-wild-type ratio no human patient has, which is precisely what makes it the most tractable demonstration rather than the most representative one.

nodes.description: Heterozygous variants alter TUBB4A, the brain-specific beta-tubulin 4A isotype. Unlike the cortical-malformation tubulinopathies, the affected isotype's critical expression is in oligodendrocytes and in basal ganglia and cerebellar neurons rather than in migrating cortical neurons. The variants perturb microtubule polymerization and the mutant subunit's incorporation into the microtubule network, and in silico the mutant heterodimers rarely adopt the straight conformation of wild type. Crucially the perturbation is not uniform: variants causing dystonia and variants causing H-ABC have divergent molecular effects, which is what makes this a genuinely pleiotropic locus rather than a single mechanism read out at different severities.

genetic_context.description: Disease alleles are heterozygous missense variants. The mechanism class is recorded as UNKNOWN deliberately, and the reason is specific to this locus: the two clinical poles have DIFFERENT molecular effects, so a single functional_impact_category cannot be correct for the gene as a whole. Severity does track with the ratio of mutant to preserved wild-type tubulin in an allelic mouse series, which is a dose-dependent dominant effect, but whether that is dominant-negative poisoning or a gain of an aberrant function has not been resolved and may differ between the dystonia and H-ABC alleles. See the gap_tubb4a_pleiotropy_mechanism discussion.

nodes.description: A parallel neuronal arm. Basal ganglia and cerebellar neurons degenerate, producing the atrophy that gives H-ABC the second half of its name and that underlies the dystonia, choreoathetosis, rigidity and ataxia of the clinical picture. Mouse modelling shows the degeneration is genuinely neuronal as well as glial, so this is not simply a consequence of the myelin defect. In the milder adult-onset dystonia form, this arm dominates and the myelin arm may be clinically silent.

nodes.description: Oligodendrocytes fail to produce and maintain normal myelin. The microtubule-dependent step identified in the mouse model is transport of Mbp (myelin basic protein) mRNA from the oligodendrocyte soma out to the myelin sheath - a cargo-delivery function that a destabilized microtubule network cannot perform. The result is hypomyelination rather than demyelination: myelin is never adequately laid down, which is why brain imaging at the time of developmental loss shows hypomyelination.

nodes.description: The clinical endpoint, and the reason this disorder is described as progressive where the cortical-malformation tubulinopathies are static. The decline reflects four anatomically distinct systems failing together: pyramidal tracts (spasticity, brisk reflexes, Babinski), extrapyramidal system (rigidity, dystonia, choreoathetosis, oculogyric crisis, perioral dyskinesia), cerebellum (ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria) and bulbar function (dysarthria, dysphonia, swallowing). Rate of progression varies with disease severity.

nodes.description: A graded allelic series that establishes the dose relationship underpinning the therapeutic strategy: severity correlates with mutant Tubb4a expression and with relative preservation of wild-type tubulin. The D249N/KO animals provide the treatment substrate for the ASO experiment.

Establishes that the model degenerates both glia and neurons, which is the evidence for curating the myelin and neurodegeneration arms as parallel branches rather than treating basal ganglia and cerebellar atrophy as secondary to demyelination.

nodes.description: The first disease-modifying strategy, and preclinical only. The rationale comes from an allelic mouse series showing that disease severity correlates with mutant Tubb4a expression and with relative preservation of wild-type tubulin - so lowering the mutant transcript should help even without repairing it. A single intracerebroventricular dose of a Tubb4a-targeted ASO in postnatal Tubb4a D249N/KO mice drastically extended lifespan, improved motor phenotypes, reduced seizures, prevented myelin and oligodendrocyte loss, and recovered visual evoked potential latencies. A stated limitation is that the ASO fails to reach cerebellar granule neurons by any tested route, so the cerebellar arm of the disease may be untreated by this approach. There is no human trial; this must not be curated anywhere as an available therapy.
